tier_reason: Public harness research/benchmark/perf/bench.py with the Rust references in research/benchmark/perf/rust-ref/ (binarytrees.rs, treealloc.rs) and raw per-run JSON (results/2026-09-08-m4pro-victory-1330.json, whose numbers match the page: 133.9 vs 381.8 ms at d17, 580.8 vs 1825.9 ms at d19); rustc flags opt-level=3, lto, codegen-units=1 and the Apple M4 Pro CPU are stated, so the native comparison against ordinary Rust is reproducible.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Native output vs ordinary hand-written Rust on Apple M4 Pro (almide 0.62.0, 2026-09-08, median of 9 interleaved runs): binarytrees d17 134 ms vs 382 ms (0.35x time), d19 581 vs 1826 ms (0.32x); treealloc d20 112 vs 375 ms (0.30x), d21 221 vs 748 ms (0.30x). With the region window turned off (ALMIDE_REGION_OFF=1) the same Almide source is 1.10-1.26x slower than the Rust reference. ubuntu-latest CI runner (2026-10-03, almide 0.66.0 dev): binarytrees 0.581 (d17), treealloc 0.365 (d20). Arithmetic kernels (2026-07-30, rustc 1.96.1): n-body and spectral-norm 1.00x, fasta 1.16x and FFT 1.18x slower than Rust. Wasm leg: README ledger (2026-09-29, embedded wasm host vs native binary, min of 2x5 interleaved) gives wasm/native ratios of 0.67x (mapbuild) to 1.96x (listbuild_append), e.g. treealloc 1.04x, binarytrees 1.07x, nbody 1.10x, fft 1.53x; these ratios are on the README, not on BENCHMARKS.md, whose older dated wasm paragraph still describes FFT (~3,500x) and mandelbrot (~130x) cliffs.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: almide --release (emits Rust, cargo release profile opt-level=3 + LTO) vs handwritten Rust built by bench.py with rustc -C opt-level=3 -C lto=yes -C codegen-units=1; median of 9 interleaved runs after warmup; byte-identical stdout verified before timing. rustc 1.96.1 is stated for the 2026-07-30 scoreboard; the 2026-09-08 victory JSON records almide 0.62.0 but no rustc version (README says CI builds with 1.96.0).
corrections.caveats: Off the category baseline: the comparison is native Rust output, not TypeScript/JS in V8 or C++ via Emscripten, and the wasm output is only compared with Almide's own native binary, never with JS/V8 or an Emscripten build. The whole win is one optimization (the region window, a thread-local bump arena rewound once per check(make(d)) tree) against a Rust reference that deliberately pays malloc/free per Box node; a Rust program using an arena (bumpalo/typed-arena, as Benchmarks Game Rust entries do) would close most of the gap (the same document shows a Zig arena at 88 ms vs Almide 72 ms at d16). Two workloads, one mechanism. The ratio is allocator-dependent (0.581 and 0.365 on the ubuntu-latest runner vs 0.35 and 0.30 on macOS). The M4 Pro columns were measured on 0.62.0 and not re-measured. The README's third victory row (fannkuchredux 0.21/0.12 via parallel fan) compares a threaded Almide run with a one-thread Rust reference and should not be cited. Self-reported by the project.

notes: Numbers on docs/project/BENCHMARKS.md match the raw JSON in the repo and the harness and Rust references are public, so A stands for the native-vs-Rust claim. Shortcomings to record: off-category baseline (no JS/V8 or Emscripten comparison), win comes only from an arena vs a malloc-per-node Rust reference, allocator-dependent ratio, unequal threaded fannkuchredux row on the README.

tier_reason: First-party mitata run with public code (benchmark/transform.js, build.sh flags), but the README numbers carry no CPU model, Node.js version or emcc version; the 'AMD 4650G' line comes from the older benchmark/README.md on the master branch / v6.2.3 tag, which describes a different harness (10,000 iterations, ops/sec, four fixture sizes), and that file no longer exists on the default develop branch.

corrections.hardware: Not stated for the current README (mitata) numbers. The 'AMD 4650G 6 cores - 12 threads/ 32GB memory' spec is in benchmark/README.md on the master branch and v6.2.3 tag, which belongs to an older ops/sec harness; that file is absent from the default develop branch.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: emcc -O3 -flto -msimd128 -DNDEBUG -std=gnu++98 -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti (pugixml and core), Embind adapter at -std=gnu++17, linked with emmalloc and --closure 1 (build.sh); emcc version, Node.js version and mitata settings of the README run are not stated (package.json: engines node >= 20.x, mitata ^1.0.34).
corrections.caveats: README itself says this is 'an unfair game for camaro': camaro extracts only the template's fields while txml, fast-xml-parser, xml-js and xml2js build the full document tree, so the comparison is not like-for-like work. The README numbers (updated 2026-08-13, 'chore: update readme with latest benchmark') state no CPU, Node.js or emcc version; the AMD 4650G spec belongs to an older harness on the master branch. Single 60 KB fixture in the current harness; the README warns that small XML strings will probably be slower than pure-JS parsers (the older benchmark README showed camaro behind on the 7 KB fixture). The library's transform() is async and can dispatch to a worker_threads pool; a single in-flight request runs on the main thread, which is what the benchmark measures.

notes: Numbers (98.94 us vs txml 491.71 us, 5.27x/25.78x/24.21x/37.02x) match the README exactly and the benchmark code is public, but the run has no stated CPU or runtime versions, so A drops to C. Shortcomings to record: unequal work (template extraction vs full-tree parse, admitted by the author), no hardware/Node version for the current numbers, single fixture, slower on small inputs.

tier_reason: Public code (benchmark.cpp, benchmark.zig, Makefile) and a stated CPU, but the Emscripten baseline is built at -O2 while the Zig contender is ReleaseFast, compiler versions are unstated (Zig '0.13+', emsdk 'latest'), each row is a single run with no variance, and the 1.29x margin rests on one runtime (WasmEdge); first-party numbers with a handicapped baseline are C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Zig to WasmEdge 15,305 ops/sec vs C++ (em++ -O2) to WasmEdge 11,855 ops/sec, about 1.29x (derived from page data); Go to WasmEdge 3,230 ops/sec. Only the WasmEdge row is reported for Zig wasm; C++ wasm on other runtimes: Wasmer LLVM 11,160, Wasmtime 6,988, Wasmer Cranelift 6,911 ops/sec. The README note that Zig WASM is 'nearly matching C++ optimized native' is contradicted by its own numbers: C++ optimized native (-O3 -march=native) is 49,279 ops/sec, about 3.2x faster than Zig wasm (derived from page data); Zig wasm instead matches Zig native ReleaseFast (15,386 ops/sec).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Zig: zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast -target wasm32-wasi (Zig version only given as 0.13+). C++ wasm baseline: em++ -std=c++20 -O2 (emsdk 'latest', version unstated), no hardening flags. C++ native: g++ -std=c++20 -O2 plus OpenSSF hardening flags (_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3, _GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS, stack protector) for 'standard', -O3 -march=native -mtune=native -flto -DNDEBUG plus the same hardening flags for 'optimized'. Go: GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build (Go 1.24+). Runs pinned with taskset -c 0; WasmEdge run with --enable-jit.
corrections.caveats: Unequal optimisation levels: the Zig WASM is ReleaseFast (LLVM -O3, no safety checks) while the Emscripten C++ WASM is -O2. Compiler and runtime versions are not stated. Single toy microbenchmark (64x64 u64 matmul + FNV-1a), one run per row, no variance or repeat count. Zig wasm is reported on WasmEdge only. Not run in V8, so it shows nothing against the TypeScript/JS baseline. The README note claiming Zig WASM nearly matches C++ optimized native is wrong by its own figures (3.2x slower). 0 stars, 8 commits all on 2025-09-01.

notes: Sources implement the same algorithm and print the chained result, so the evidence is not invalid, but the baseline is built at a lower optimisation level than the contender and every row is one run, so A drops to C. Shortcomings to record: -O2 vs ReleaseFast, single run, WasmEdge only, unversioned toolchains, misleading README note, toy repo with 0 stars.
